utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could the Registrar please call the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi, Ms. Sutherland and Mr. Vos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, My name is Toma Fila. I am here with Ms. Lopovic and Mr. Petrovic. We appear as Defence counsel for Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? We will now start with the Prosecution evidence on the issue of nationality. We plan to have a break at around 10 o'clock, then resume at 10.20 and then we should finish by 11.30, if it is possible, because at 12 o'clock we have a status conference in another case: do you think you can manage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will go through the questions which we should discuss with the Defence counsel here in court, but I would first of all ask the Prosecutor to call witnesses on the question of nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. We will not be calling any witnesses this morning. I think everything has been agreed to in the form of stipulations between ourselves and the Defence. We will, however, be tendering some documentary evidence in support of some issues, related to nationality. We will also submit a number of other documents just to complete our case. I can proceed -- there are a number of things that we would present. At this time, the first exhibit which will be 112, we have 13 photographic albums which depict an overview of the exhumation and autopsies process on 12 of the representative persons from the grave. We would introduce these albums at this time and I will introduce each one with a separate number identifying the individual. The first one, which will be exhibit 112, is the overview of the Ovcara grave mass exhumation. Exhibit 113 is the album related to Josip Kozul. Exhibit 114 is the album related to Josip Balog. Exhibit 115 is the album related to Pavao Jurisic. Exhibit 116 is the album related to Mihajlo Zera. Exhibit 117 is the album related to Martin Jakubovski. Exhibit 118 is the album related to Sinisa Glavasevic. Exhibit 119 is the album related to Hrvoje Ljubas. Exhibit 120 is the album related to Sinisa Veber. Exhibit 121 is the album related to Dragutin Bosanac. Exhibit 122 is the album related to Igor Kacic. Exhibit 123 is the album related to Tomislav Baumgartner. Exhibit 124 is the album related to Zeljko Jurisic. At this time, I would tender those items. We have copies of these which have previously been provided to the court and the Defence in conjunction with our pre-trial submissions of evidence. In relation to these items, and the next two items, the court had already ruled that these could be admitted on 19 January in the pre-trial hearing. There was some discussion on them at that time, but now we are just merely formally tendering them. The next item is the video compilation which depicts the Ovcara exhumation which was shown in court on 17 March 1998, in conjunction with the testimony of Dr. Clyde Snow. This has already been viewed, but at that time we did not actually tender it. We would do so now. That would be Prosecutor's exhibit 125. That is this item. Then the next item is a copy of a 1:100,000 scale map of the entire Vukovar region which I believe may have been referred to at some point in testimony. We would tender this as Prosecutor's exhibit 126. Again, all of these items 112 through to 124, are the albums, 125 and 126, have previously been provided both to the Defence and to the court. The next item will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 127A and B. A is the audio recording of the statement given by Mr. Dokmanovic on 27 June 1997, after his arrest when he was en route from Cepin in Croatia to The Hague and 127B is the transcript of that statement. The audio tape is being obtained from the evidence unit -- we do not yet have that in court this morning. We will put that in the record as soon as we receive it. At this time we can submit 127B, which is the transcript of that, and again copies of this have already been provided to the Defence, and to the court, and I believe the audio tapes have actually already been provided. The next exhibit, your Honours, is Prosecutor's evidence 128A and B -- 128A is three videotapes of the statement given by Mr. Dokmanovic at the Scheveningen prison on 26 and 27 November 1997 -- there is a misprint, sorry -- and this is 128A, the transcript of that interview will be introduced as Prosecutor's exhibit 128B. The next item is Prosecutor's exhibit 129. This is offered in support of the admissions obtained relative to the exhumation and autopsies -- this is the report of Dr. Yvonne Milewski as to the pathological findings arising from the post-mortem examinations of bodies recovered from the Ovcara grave site with special emphasis on these 12 representative persons. We have made copies of all these items here and we have those here in court. We can provide those perhaps at the conclusion of this process, just to expedite things. The Defence has received, I believe, all these items in advance, except for a couple of things, but we will provide everything -- sufficient copies for all of the judges and for the Registry and for the Defence. The next items -- and this is in support of the admissions in relation to the nationality -- these are the personal documents recovered from the bodies of 45 individuals exhumed from the Ovcara grave site -- this goes to nationality and identification of individuals. I will go through with each of these documents -- they will be given an individual number. The documents were obtained from the bodies so there is some odour associated with them -- these were documents that had been in the grave for five years before the exhumation, so as a result of the decomposition of the bodies, the documents have also a smell. We have tried to mitigate that as much as possible -- they were already placed in plastic and we have additionally placed them into zip lock closed bags, plastic bags as well, but we will go through that as quickly as we can. We have them in a box. If it is to your Honours' pleasure, we can leave them in the box and submit it as one item, or we can do them individually, but again there will be some smell associated with doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You do not have to submit them individually -- you can just give us the whole box.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I will go through each one by name and the exhibit number. We will submit it as a box. We have photocopies of them which we can provide to the Defence and the court so that it will not be necessary to go into the originals in the courtroom. Exhibit 130 would be documents which were taken from the body of Mihaela Balas, which is a prescription and doctor's note. Exhibit 131 is an SFRY identification card for Josip Balog. Exhibit 132 is an SFRY identification card for Ivan Plavsic. Exhibit 133 is an SFRY identification card for Pavao Jurisic . Exhibit 134 is an identification card for Stjepan Sarik. Exhibit 135 is a medical document in the name of Nedeljko Hlevnjak. Exhibit 136 is a medical document in the name of Tihomir Traljic. Exhibit 137 is an identification card in the name of Ivan Herman. Exhibit 138 is an SFRY identification card in the name of Mihaljo Zera. Exhibit 139 is a Vukovar medical centre identification card in the name of Mihaljo Zera. Exhibit 140 is an identification card in the name of Mufad Omerovic. Exhibit 141 is a prescription in the name of Josip Rapustic. Exhibit 142 is an SFRY identification in the name of Josip Zeljko. Exhibit 143 is an SFRY identification card in the name of Pero Simunic. Exhibit 144 is an identification card from the Vukovar Prosecutor's Office of Kresimir Kelava. Exhibit 145 is an identification card for Tomislav Mihovic. Exhibit 146 is an identification card for Tomislav Bajnrauh. Exhibit 147 is an identification card for Marko Lucic. Exhibit 148 is an SFRY identification card for Tihomir Tomasic. Exhibit 149 is an SFRY identification card for Drago Jurendic. Exhibit 150 is an SFRY identification for Ivica Horvat. Exhibit 151 is an SFRY identification card for Petar Turk. Exhibit 156 is an SFRY identification card for Darko Tisljaric . Sorry, 152. Exhibit 153 is an SFRY identification card for Mihael Janic. Exhibit 154 is an SFRY identification card for Vinko Andrijanic. Exhibit 155 is an identification card for Salvador Rimac. Exhibit 156 is an SFRY identification card for Mihael Janic. Exhibit 157 is an identification card for Zdravko Mikulic. Exhibit 158 is a medical document for Vedran Galic. Exhibit 159 is an SFRY identification card for Borislav Kostovic. Exhibit 160, personal documents in the name of Dragutin Bosanac. Exhibit 161 is an SFRY identification card for Dragan Granic. Exhibit 162 is an SFRY identification card for Anton Virges. Exhibit 163 is an SFRY identification card for Josip Dragun. Exhibit 164 is an SFRY identification card for Karlo Rohacek. Exhibit 165 is an SFRY identification card for Sasa Dudar. Exhibit 166 is an identification card for Duka Baric. Exhibit 167 is an SFRY identification card for Stanoja Cupic. Exhibit 168 is an identification document for Igor Kacic. Exhibit 169 is an SFRY identification card for Branislav Graf. Exhibit 170 is an SFRY identification card for Borislav Garvanovic. Exhibit 171 is an SFRY identification card for Mikailo Vasic. Exhibit 172 is an identification card for Tomislav Baumgartner. Exhibit 173 is a medical document in the name of Dragutin Friscic. Exhibit 174 is an SFRY identification card in the name of Branimir Polovina and then exhibit 175 is a prescription document in the name of Zeljko Jurisic. We would offer all of these items in their entirety exhibits 130 to 175, again in the box and we will provide copies of the documents to both Defence and the court. The next items are copies of international agreements which were entered into by the Croatian Government in the period between June and December 1991, and these were obtained at the request of the Trial Chamber. We will offer these in globo as exhibit 176. Your Honours, I understand that there was a correction which was made in relation to one of the names which I just stated -- this was on exhibit 152, the name appeared on my printout as Darko Tisljaric and it should have been Nikola Pinter -- that was exhibit 152. I am sorry, your Honours, it is exhibit 153, instead of Mihaljo Janjic it should have been Nikola Pinter -- exhibit 152 was correct, it should have been Darko Tisljaric. The next items --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I did not get this. I do not have it. Could I please get this, because it is important?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You mean the correction of the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, the document -- I am referring to the document, the agreement, yes, yes, the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Again, it was our intention to provide everything at the conclusion. We can give you a copy. The next items are those related to the ethnicity of seven persons upon which the Prosecution and Defence could not come to agreement as to ethnicity. We did enter into an admission in relation to the other persons named in the indictment, but there were seven persons upon which agreement could not be reached. We have sought documentation from the Croatian Government and the first item that we would offer would be Prosecutor's exhibit 177, which is a letter which came from the Croatian Office of Missing Persons in relation to these seven individuals. Your Honours, I am sorry, that does not seem to be in the courtroom at the moment. We will retrieve that -- it is 177A, which is the Croatian version of that and 177B will be the English version of that letter. 178A is a blank form which shows the form for questionnaires that survivors of missing persons filed with the Croatian Office of Missing Persons. This is 178A. 178B is an English translation of this document, so that, when referring to it, you may then be able to tell what the questions are, which are filled out on the completed forms, so this is 178A and B. Exhibit 179 will be a form that was filled out in relation to an individual, Duka Baric. This is not one of the individuals that was at dispute in our discussions between ourselves and the Defence. However, there were three individuals who were found in the grave who were not named in the indictment, so we have also provided documentation in relation to these three, as well as to the other seven which were in dispute. So, this is exhibit 179, Duka Baric. Exhibit 180 are documents in relation to Vjekoslav Poljak -- again, who is one of the individuals who was not named in indictment, but who has been positively identified from the grave -- it is exhibit 180. And the same applies to exhibit 181, which is for Pero Simunic. Exhibit 182 are documents related to Branko Jovanovic. Exhibit 183 are documents in relation to Goran Kitic. Exhibit 184 are documents in relation to Tihomir Loncar. Exhibit 185 are documents in relation to Polovina Branimir. Exhibit 186 are documents in relation to Tihomir Savanovic and exhibit 187 are documents in relation to Mikajilo Vasic. No document was found in relation to Stanija Kupic, so nothing has been provided in relation to him. Exhibit 188 are census figures for Vukovar municipality for the years 1971, 1981, and 1991, which indicate figures for the entire municipality, and then for 1991, the populations of the individual villages within the municipality and there is a colour map which is attached, which indicates the predominant ethnic groups in each of the towns in the Vukovar municipality, indicating where there are absolute majorities or relative majorities in the population. This would be exhibit 188. Finally, the last exhibit 189, which is a copy of the 1990 Croatian constitution. In addition to these items, there are a couple of other matters as well, that we would like to address. We have made two requests to the United Nations in New York for documents, which we are still awaiting. If we can obtain agreement of the Defence and if it is the pleasure of your Honours, we would like to supplement this after we have closed our case with these two small items that we have requested. We have asked from the United Nations for the main multi-lateral treaties and instruments of succession deposited by Croatia and the notifications by the depositor to the States, parties to the treaties, on all of them which mention or acknowledge 8 October 1991 as the effective date of Croatian independence. We were told the documents were with the Austrian Government and we made enquires through them. They indicated to us that everything had been forwarded to the United Nations, so we have put in a request to the UN and we have been told that we should get a response some time this week, but rather than delay the closing of our case, if it is agreeable to the Defence, we would supplement it when that is obtained. The other item that we have also requested from the UN is an item that was referred to in Mr. Mesic's testimony -- this was the ultimatum from General Kadijevic to the Croatian authorities which Mr. Mesic referred to as a declaration of war in which he attached to his letter to Mr. Perez de Cuellar. As soon as we obtain those, we will supplement it. At this time we would like to show a small portion of videotape, which has already been admitted as Prosecutor's exhibit 75. This is an interview with Slavko Dokmanovic which was done by Radio Television Belgrade shortly after 20 November 1991. There was some discussion about this during our pre-trial submission of evidence and the court determined that this could go in as it is, so at this time we would like to show that to the court, and then we will tender the evidence and that would conclude our case. If that is ready, we can show that now. We will provide copies of everything to the Defence in the interim so they have an opportunity if there is any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with that, but I just want to ask you one thing. Could we run the entire tape that has been given to me, because the tape that the Prosecutor gave me contains other interviews made on the same date and, in the tape of the Prosecution it says "former President of the municipality of Vukovar" -- former President. If the Prosecutor says they want to establish the truth, they should play that tape, too -- that part of the tape, too. It is their exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think there is some confusion as to tapes. What we provided to Mr. Fila in pre-trial discovery process were all of the interviews that we had with Mr. Dokmanovic over a long period of time. These go all the way until 1996. What we did in terms of this compilation that we have submitted as Prosecutor's exhibit 75 was place only the ones that were made at the time of the conclusion of the battle of Vukovar and this was the only interview from that period. All of the others occur at a later time. If the Defence requests, we can certainly make that available, but that is not on this tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is precisely from that period, the 21st, the interview with the French man, and it says "former President of the municipality" there; is that right? Yes -- it is that period, not earlier, not later -- that is the period in question -- November 1991, your exhibit, so if you want to be fair, show both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We will show this one at this time and we will try to obtain the one that Mr. Fila is discussing, we are happy to provide that to the court as well. We would supplement that after the fact. At this time, we are ready to proceed with the one that was made immediately after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is it agreeable to you? In any case, it will be shown -- not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I agree with it, but I do not find it agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is clear that the Prosecutor has committed himself to show this tape, but not today, because I understand it is not available now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour -- we can get it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We can try to get it this morning. I think the reason it was not included, it was a very short segment, it is not clear but we are happy to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We could have a break or maybe a break at 9.30, and then maybe you can show that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, that is fine. At this time, we would request to show the portion that I have referred to a moment ago. I believe this is at the very beginning of this tape. All of this has previously been shown to the court. We wanted to show the last segment which is at the very end of the tape. This tape is of some length. At this time perhaps we can tender all of the items that I have discussed -- these are exhibits 125 through 189, and if there is any of these that Mr. Fila would like to see at this time that he has not seen previously, we can provide those.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would only like to see when these international agreements were signed and which ones are you referring to -- before 19 November? That is what this trial is about -- 20 November -- or are they dated later and also these forms are all from 1995 -- not before 1991, so I would like to have a look at that, too, for those six or seven Serbs. Please, your Honour, I wish to draw your attention to -- either intentionally or unintentionally there is a confusion between "ethnicity" and "nationality" -- not all Serbs lived in Croatia or do they live in Serbia now; not all Croats live in Croatia. In Belgrade we have about 20,000 citizens who are Croats -- they are Yugoslav citizens, but Croats by ethnicity. These documents from 1992 show something completely different. We wanted to show before 1991, before they were killed in Ovcara -- of course, they were not supposed to be killed and I already said that -- they were ethnic Serbs -- they either were or not. I am not talking about their nationality in terms of the State whose citizens they were. That is the question. That is what I would like to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: These forms address that specific issue, your Honour. It refers to their citizenship, their nationality or ethnic origin, and their religion -- all three, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When are these forms from? What is the date on these forms?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The documents, your Honours, have different dates on them. It was when the family members filled them out. Some of them are from right after the battle, some of them are somewhat later, but, your Honours, it would be our contention that the ethnic origin of a person would not change from 1992 to 1996 -- their citizenship might very well change, and, in fact, all of these persons list citizenship from Croatia, but their ethnic origin or nationality, as it was called in Yugoslavia, would remain the same. I think it reflects that. I think if Mr. Fila sees these it will clear it up. Perhaps it would be helpful for him to look at these. I think this will address his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Alright.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The agreements -- we, too, are keen to look at the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: These are copies of the agreements here. This was offered as Prosecutor's exhibit 176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While you are distributing or circulating the agreements and the other documents, may I ask you a question about an issue which you have just addressed -- the difference between "nationality" or "ethnicity" and citizenship; was there any law on citizenship in Croatia at the relevant time? Was there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the time, from the time that Yugoslavia was created, all of the citizens of Yugoslavia had citizenship both in Yugoslavia and in the republic in which they lived, so all these persons, it refers to their citizenship as being that from Croatia. Nationality was not restricted to any Serb republic -- I think this is what Mr. Fila was discussing -- someone who had Serb nationality could live in Serbia, Croatia or Bosnia, so, in effect, nationality and ethnicity are one and the same. Citizenship was something different and citizenship applied to the republic in which they lived, but it made no indication of their ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, therefore, somebody could be a citizen of Croatia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Dual citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the time prior to the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, everyone had citizenship in the Republic and as a Yugoslav citizen. After the break-up of Yugoslavia, of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, people now have only citizenship in the independent nation in which they live, be it Croatia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, or Slovenia, Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did Croatia pass any law on citizenship after the break-up --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It is contained in the constitution of 1990 which we have offered as Prosecutor's exhibit 189 and then there is an additional document which is the law of citizenship of Croatia of 1991. Just a moment, your Honour -- I believe after the break we can attempt to supplement the record with that law as well in response to your request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The first expert that you will be hearing tomorrow is professor of constitutional law from our faculty of law. He is going to explain this properly to you. All of us in the SFRY together had citizenship of the SFRY and that was called external citizenship. That is citizenship that was valid in the outside world, so to speak. Within the SFRY we had republics and these republics had internal citizenship which was for internal use only. Every citizen of the SFRY, you can see that in the law on attorneys, the law on courts, et cetera, the citizen of any part of Yugoslavia was allowed to practise law anywhere, for example. In our red passports it said that we were citizens of the SFRY, not Serbia, Croatia, Macedonia, et cetera, but what I am objecting as far as these documents are concerned -- please, I wish to draw your attention to that regardless of whether you are going to accept them as exhibits or not -- the forms that have a later date than the date concerning this trial are the forms that are being offered, and I asked the Prosecutor to give me documents showing the ethnic background of these persons -- not where they lived, what republic they lived in -- for these people before 1991 and you have that in the lists that were provided by the Croat States and you can also get it from church documents. We Serbs were baptised in Serb Orthodox churches. As you know today, it is our Easter, and your Easter was a week ago. I have documents for these seven persons from the church so that is the exhibit that I asked the Prosecutor to provide -- that these people were baptised as Croats before 1991, just as I am going to show them that they were baptised as Serb Orthodox when they were born, not bring you new documents that will be produced by my State or their State. That is relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In any case, as for the forms, let us wait for the breaks so we can look at the various forms and we will resume discussion of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: These are the forms that were referred to as Prosecutor's exhibits 178 through 187. At this time, I believe we are ready to proceed with the video of the interview concerning Mr. Dokmanovic. If it can be run at this time. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not receiving a translation of this, your Honour. Perhaps if we could re-roll it and start with the translation as well. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Today, Vukovar is the most devastated city on earth and that is the question that we are discussing with the mayor of Vukovar, Slavko Dokmanovic. What are we supposed to do? Answer: Unfortunately, it is true that Vukovar is the most devastated city in the world -- the city that was an example of cleanliness, of order, it no longer exists. We are going to do our best to rebuild the city and intensive work is being done on that score in two directions. First of all, a civilian government is going to be set up, today or perhaps tomorrow, and the city is going to be rebuilt and preparations are under way in a few directions. First of all, it is necessary to restore the city, then we are going to clear up the ruins and, according to the project we have envisaged, we are going to build a new city and I sincerely hope it is never going to be a Ustashe town again, it will be a real Serb town where all citizens will live freely. It has been a city of refugees for months. Already in June, Serbs found refuge here as they were flowing --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is the tape. I think that was the commentary by the reporter after the conclusion of the interview. I would just ask if the videotape can be rerun and I would ask for a translation of the caption which appears under Mr. Dokmanovic's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you about the date of this interview -- I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This was 21 or 22 November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It was actually shown on 22 November in Belgrade, so it is not clear if it actually happened on that day or on the 22nd when the interview was made. If this can be run and I will indicate the point. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic President of the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, if we can take the break we will try to resolve these other outstanding matters. We should be able to conclude that upon our return, if that is acceptable to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: How much time would you need when we resume --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just a very few moments. We can play this videotape that the Defence has requested, we can show -- we will supplement the record with this letter from the Croatian authorities in relation to all the individuals, which we have marked as Prosecutor's exhibit 177A and B, and then I believe there may be some discussion about some of our exhibits, but other than that, this will conclude everything that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We could maybe break now and resume at 10 o'clock -- is that fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure we even need that much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So that you can take a look at the documents. We have 35 minutes. We will resume at 10 o'clock. (9.25 a.m.). (A short break). (10.00 a.m.).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I raise two issues? First of all, I went through the documents collected in exhibit 176 -- a group of agreements -- and I came across a document, Joint Commission to Trace Missing Persons and Mortal Remains. I have a small query, namely, whether it is correct to say here on the heading, the title 6 of this document; "Rules of Procedure and Plan of Operations 16 December 1991 amended on 31 July 1991" -- is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure. I do not have the document in front of me. Let me check very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It must be 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think it must be -- it is a misprint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That was my first query. Then we would like to ask both parties about the special attire worn by Mr. Dokmanovic when he gave that interview we saw this morning on tape on 21 or 22 November. We just saw the tape this morning. We noted that he was wearing special attire -- he was not wearing a suit, a dark suit or whatever -- whatever his capacity, so we would like to ask both parties about the nature of this sort of camouflage suit he was wearing, and whether or not it was different from the one he was wearing on the different occasion, on 20 November, when we saw him, whether this was the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the territory where the operations were held, which you are going to see whether it was an international conflict, an internal conflict or whatever, there was no water and no electricity -- people did not take baths. What Mr. Dokmanovic was wearing both on 20 and 21, he was wearing for two or three months, both before and after the events, and that is the same thing I showed you on the first day, with his alibi, and that is the same thing the Prosecution showed to the witnesses, Cakalic and Berghofer, as being his uniform on the photograph. You have those in the Prosecution's evidence. It is a hunting suit, in fact, -- a hunting uniform -- and when I start bringing up my witnesses, I am going to show you this as proof. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is certainly our position that this was a military outfit of some type. We have heard testimony on this issue from one of the witnesses who testified confidentially -- I do not recall what his number was -- who had served in the Serb paramilitary. He said everyone was doing a mish-mash of uniforms and I think that the fact that he elected to wear camouflage clothing shows very clearly that he intended to appear as some type of military or paramilitary role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time we are ready to supplement the additional items that we discussed earlier. We have now the letter which was returned from the Government of the Republic of Croatia in relation to the seven persons upon whom we requested information, and I have a copy of it -- 177 -- exhibit 177A is the version in Croatian and 177B is the English translation of that document. I have provided this to Mr. Fila at the conclusion of the break. At this time, also, we have obtained a copy of the law on Croatian citizenship. I have an English version of this -- I am not sure if I have a Croatian version yet. We can supplement that later today. This is the law on citizenship which was enacted on 26 June 1991. I understand that there were amendments made to it in 1992 and in 1993, and I do not have those, but I do have the original version of the law which was enacted in June 1991 and we would enter that now as Prosecution's exhibit 190. At this time, also, we have the videotape which Mr. Fila was requesting to be shown and we can show that at this time. This appeared on French television on channel TFI on 29 November, the film was apparently made on 28 November 1991. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Why not? They have nothing to look for here, no business to be here. They will answer to the law. There are just Serbs returning, 2,500 people who, despite everything, live in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you replay that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is not the video in question. Once again, we have the uniform that the Prosecutor calls a uniform. Eight days after this event, you will see he is wearing the same thing, the same clothing that you call a paramilitary uniform. But the particular tape that I asked for has a caption underneath where it says: "Former President of the municipality of Vukovar" and that was on the tape that the Prosecutor provided, but they are not going to show it because it does not suit their purposes. It says "former" on the caption underneath. I will show you, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I resent the allegation that we are not going to show it. We made a good faith effort based on Mr. Fila's description in court as to what tape he was talking about, and that is what we showed. I clearly do not know which segment of video he is talking about. If he can show it to us, we will be happy to provide it to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The section is in Belgrade -- I have it. I received it from the Prosecutors and my man will be bringing it here tomorrow, so I will show it to you tomorrow -- just the caption which says: "Former President of the municipality" -- that is the point, not the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could run the tape again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can reshow this very brief segment, and if translation can be made of the caption which appears again under the picture of Mr. Dokmanovic in this video. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It says "mayor of Vukovar" in the caption: "They have no business to be here and they will answer to the law. For the moment, it is only the Serbs who are coming back, 2,500 people who are living in Vukovar, despite everything."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe that that was all of the loose strings that we needed to tie up after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, we would tender all of those exhibits 125 through 190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no objection from Mr. Fila, I understand, to the tendering of those exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that I should like to repeat that all the questionnaires for the seven individuals were made up in 1994 onwards -- both in Croatia and in Serbia. When you are born, you get a birth certificate and, with that birth certificate, you carry all your life and have it until you die. That is the only proof of who is who and who is what and I ask the Prosecution to show that type of evidence and not a questionnaire of three, four or five years after the events. As far as interstate agreements go, the remarks you made, I have nothing against all this being adopted, but they are not interstate agreements. Thank you very much, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the birth certificates that Mr. Fila is referring to, in the period during which all of this occurred, in which most of these people went missing, Vukovar was totally destroyed. Most of the documents that were in Vukovar have gone missing -- hospital records -- other items which would help in the identification of persons went missing. The Croatian authorities made every attempt to find these documents after the exhumation to assist in identification, as did the Office of the Prosecutor. They are gone -- some of them were destroyed, some of them were apparently removed after 1991 in an effort to conceal the identity of persons. So I am afraid this is the best information that we have available and certainly, if we had birth certificates for these people, we would be happy to provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall try and find what has disappeared through the Croats. Now, you have given us a list, a census of the population of 1991, and so on. This implies people, individuals -- a consensus is made up of individuals. If you have these population censuses, then you have these people alive, you have their names and surnames, including the people we are talking about and it could not have disappeared, because the Prosecution has these names. So, when the population stated what they were by virtue of their nationality, nationality was one of the columns to fill in on the form. If the Croat republic wants to give you this, you will see in the population census you will have them by name and nationality and religion, so he can be a Serb, a Croat, a Yugoslav, a non defined -- he can declare himself in all these different ways, he can be an Orthodox, a Catholic, nothing else. So that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Mr. Fila can find them and produce them to court, I am sure it will be of benefit to all of us. Your Honours, we tender the last video that was shown as exhibit 191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the evidence for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I suggest that we now move on to some housekeeping matters before we adjourn, and I will now turn to Mr. Fila. First of all, a few questions. We have received, and we are grateful to you for submitting various documents, including the draft order of witnesses. Am I correct in inferring from your lists that you intend to call 16 witnesses in April, and 27 in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, four witnesses were for the video link, but in our discussions with the Registrar, we came to realise that it would be better to have both in May for a whole day, and in that sense I informed the Registrar that it is, for practical purposes, the better solution -- to bring all these witnesses from Belgrade and to get them over in one day, so that you have four less, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Four less in April. I am happy that you accepted the suggestion of the Registrar. We also were going to ask you to put together all the witnesses to be heard through video link, and hear them in May. Actually, we would like to suggest 18 May, if this is convenient for the parties. We will then have only 12 witnesses in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you call some other witnesses you intended to call in May -- can you call them now in April? Some of your witnesses to be called in May, could they be called in April?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that this number is too great, because four of these witnesses are expert witnesses, and there will be a lot of questions from the Prosecution side, because I would like to hear all the experts at the start, and that is how I conduct my Defence cases in my own country, so that everybody knows what we are talking about and then we talk to the witnesses. The first expert that you are going to hear after my opening statement has to do with matters of the constitution, what constitutions exist, what they are like and citizenship. The other expert is on international conflicts and they are both here. The third and fourth witnesses are experts in the realm of history -- Serbs up to the Second World War and the Serbs from the Second World War onwards. This will take a lot of time. I do not have many questions to ask, but I am sure the Prosecution will. As far as the witnesses are concerned, we can shorten their time, of course, depending upon questions from the Prosecution, but I do not think we will get through even the four we have -- let us hope we will. I have something else to ask you. For three witnesses, I have asked safe conduct. I have not received a reply from the Prosecution as to whether they agree. (redacted) (redacted). I would like to have an okay from you, because without these assurances, they will not be able to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I was about to ask you a question about the witnesses who are asking for safe conduct. (redacted), you mentioned four witnesses -- (redacted) (redacted), (redacted). You are asking for four safe conducts? Actually, it is five -- there is also (redacted). What about these five names?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The situation, your Honours, has changed, and in our talks with the Prosecutor we concluded that it would not be a good idea to have (redacted) to come here and to ask for safe conduct for him. I am sure the reasons are understandable. The witness (redacted) does not ask for safe conduct, because he lives on Croatian territory and there is no problem there. (redacted) (redacted). I am not putting forward (redacted) at this point. I think he would be on the video link if we should so decide. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (redacted) and this was an additional request from me to you. I do not think there will be any problem in allowing them safe conduct, because it does not make the work of the court any more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (redacted). Sorry for my bad pronunciation. I see that the response from the Prosecutor was due by 22 April, namely, on Wednesday, about the Defence motion for safe conduct. Am I correct in saying this? This is according to my calculation. You submitted a response concerning the video link, but no response about the safe conduct. I wonder whether you could state your position now so we can clarify this matter, or whether you need two more days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we are almost in a position -- we were going to comply according to the time requirements, but I think our position -- we are a little puzzled by one of the witnesses, because we understood he wants safe conduct because he does not have a passport -- we may be wrong about that, but that seemed to be the position with one of the witnesses,

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: (redacted). Just going on to the video link, if your Honours wish to have the video link because you consider it more economical, or efficient or whatever, then I suppose I do not have much to say about it. Our position is that we would prefer that video links be limited to those circumstances where it is simply not possible for any other way for the evidence to be given; in other words, that it is not possible for the witness to travel to The Hague. If that is established and in those circumstances, we raise no objection to that. But the position of the Prosecution certainly -- and it is a position we will state -- is; we much prefer the witness to come before the Tribunal to testify before your Honours, with your Honours' ability to observe demeanour and the control of the witnesses is much greater and that is far preferable to video link testimony. Our position, your Honours, is that notwithstanding efficiency, that the far better course is always to have the witness testify here in person. So, our general objection perhaps falls away if your Honours prefer to do it by video link in terms of efficiency, but we make the observation that it is better to encourage witnesses to come to The Hague. Otherwise, a situation could easily develop in future cases where the whole process is by video link and, in our submission, the effect of testifying by that process is far less satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We share your concern about the resort to video link testimony. On the other hand, I understand from Mr. Fila there are compelling reasons as to why the witnesses are not prepared to come over here and give evidence in court -- I am asking you about the video link.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, (redacted), we have cleared up that case. Mr. Licina is an old man. Let me remind you, he is a witness that the Prosecutor said was one of the individuals who was at Ovcara -- he is very old. I do not know whether they will be able to bring him even to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I hesitate to cut short Mr. Fila. I need to make it absolutely clear that, in relation to the witness Mr. Mile Bakic, Mr. (redacted), Mr. Ilija Koncarevic and Mr. Zivko Licina, there is absolutely no objection -- those matters have been dealt with before -- it is the addition of the other 12 we are concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think it is eight -- there are 12 altogether. There are four plus eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Eight -- you have misgivings about the other eight?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not know the reason why, and we believe that it is probably because it is just more efficient and easier. We accept that -- there is no question about that, but it does, in our submission, tend to detract from the effectiveness of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you restate in court the reasons why you are suggesting that the eight witnesses who should have been heard in May cannot come here to give evidence in court, but should be heard through video link conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There are two reasons. One is the lack of travelling papers -- (redacted) (redacted). You must understand one thing, your Honours: a large number of these people, when they fled from Croatia to Serbia, or to Montenegro or wherever, they were given refugee papers. You have that in the supporting material -- that is explained to you, so they have no citizenship, and if you have no citizenship, you cannot have travelling papers or travelling documents. Therefore, they cannot come even if they wanted to come. Another part, like (redacted), he is the commander of the Territorial Defence in Petrova Gora. Fear is the reason. You know the witness that Mr. Williamson brought, you know what he said about the Territorial Defence. What was his name? It was Witness Q. That is why he is afraid, but I completely agree with Mr. Niemann's attitude that it is better to bring the witnesses here than have a video link conference. But, your Honour, let us look at this from another aspect. The day that these four are heard, the four that Mr. Niemann agrees to, I am going to bring some of them, and there is no harm in hearing their voices, and if they are worth half the testimonies presented here, that is worth something, a point will have been gained. Perhaps they will help us. But, I cannot make them come -- you must believe me. That is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (redacted). You heard Mr. Williamson explain the difficulties involved in bringing witnesses here, and my difficulties are even greater. They have all three asked for protective measures as well -- after the time I asked safe conduct for them, so since then they have asked for protective measures as well -- for face distortion. You have been doing this same job -- you know how difficult it is with witnesses. I do not think there is any problem in giving them safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Fila may be assured that we will be as cooperative as we possibly can be in making the situation as easy as it can be for him to get his witnesses here. We will not do anything to interfere with that or for his testimony to be heard. It was only we were concerned we did not know the reasons. With respect to the temporary nature of their travelling documents, my experience has been that the Victims and Witness Unit seem to have a remarkable relationship with the Dutch authorities and have been able to achieve a great deal in relation to Prosecution witnesses, if they are given the time and notice, and I do not want to go into details, but they have been in circumstances much more difficult than that which Mr. Fila has explained, so I would first ask him to exhaust that avenue with them before he finally says that he cannot bring them here because of that technical problem. If witnesses refuse to come, and their testimony is important, obviously the Prosecution is not going to object to that. If witnesses are fearful, again, I would ask that the Victims and Witness Unit be given an opportunity at least to explain to the witnesses what facilities are available to them in order to offer them protection if they were to testify here in The Hague. They are most expert in their work in looking after witnesses in these circumstances and reassuring them at times when they are fearful. If all else fails, we will not object to it, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Niemann, just one more thing. It is precisely because safe conduct is an issue that I asked these three witnesses to arrive on Sunday -- to be in The Hague for three days only, while the others will be arriving tomorrow. So that this period for which safe conduct is requested, which does create certain difficulties for the Registrar, be as short as possible, from Sunday until Thursday. I cannot do more than that. Sorry, Mr. Niemann, for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The issue of safe conduct is a broader issue than just the Tribunal. This involves the Dutch Government as well. We do not know what position the Dutch Government has in relation to particular individuals, and so bringing them here does require negotiation and consultation with them. So it is not just a simple case of saying, "Well the Prosecution are being difficult." We are not being difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You do not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can proceed on the assumption that if the Dutch authorities are agreeable, the three witnesses will get safe conduct and will give testimony next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May I give some further explanation? Perhaps it is a nice thing to say and perhaps it is not, but these persons are not fearful of anyone but the Prosecution. They really want safe conduct only from the Prosecution. They want to make sure -- sorry, this is not personal about Mr. Niemann, but the Prosecutor is not going to arrest them. That is the kind of guarantee I need from you and protective measures are another thing, facial distortion, et cetera. I do not know what the Dutch Government has to do with it -- if you pass a decision or ruling saying they will not be arrested by the Prosecution, that is sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, the safe conduct in this case is not a travel document but it has the main purpose of granting immunity from prosecution. On the other hand, I think Mr. Niemann is absolutely right in saying we also need to consult with the Dutch authorities, because the Dutch authorities might have other reasons for not granting an immunity to those witnesses. So, therefore, let us see whether the Dutch authorities grant their consent and I understand that, in any case, there is no objection from the Prosecution. The Prosecution is prepared to grant immunity from prosecution to those three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will not arrest them when they are here. I do not think I can go any wider than that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I take your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, not only when they come here, but allow them to go back, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I mean the whole period of their stay in The Netherlands. We have this list of witnesses -- 16 plus 27. I wonder whether I can ask Mr. Fila whether he intends to call Mr. Dokmanovic as a witness, to give evidence on his behalf? It is just a query -- you are not required to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this period, certainly not, and his health condition is such that I would prefer deciding on this matter in May, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: How much time do you need in May, because we will probably go through the various witnesses by Tuesday of next week? Then, in May, we will have the 12 witnesses to be heard through video link conference, and all the other ones. There will therefore be 31 in May. Do you need two weeks in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to make it shorter than two weeks, but I need the cooperation of the other side, too. I am not the only one who can say that, because the cross-examination will be longer, I imagine, than the examination-in-chief. So, as you can see, according to the Defence schedule, the witnesses to be heard in May are basically alibi witnesses from the tape. As far as the general circumstances are concerned, why what happened in Croatia and how it happened -- we are going to deal with that now. So, all the experts and that. There is going to be one remaining expert, a neuro psychiatrist, and he will be heard in May, the one who is monitoring health, that will be all. Believe me, I will make an effort and you see I have been making an effort to expedite matters. I imagine we will let the Prosecution have their last word in May, too, in those two weeks, but I shall complete it in hopefully less than two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: At the end of the presentation of your case, we will have the closing statements, and I wonder whether we could finish by the end of May, because we have only two weeks in May, and I do not know whether we can have a week in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We could certainly conclude in June, as far as I am concerned we will be through in June, because we will need a day to see the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did you say June or May?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: June -- I said June for sure, but in May I will show the tapes and in June we finish for sure, no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure about May for the Prosecution. We do anticipate calling some evidence in rebuttal. I may not, but I assume we will, so I think June is more realistic in that sense. I noted Mr. Fila mentioned the psychiatrist and ask that if that evidence in any way touches upon the provisions of Rule 61A(ii)(b) that we be given notice of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no -- no, no, no, no, I would have told you that straight away at the very outset -- no, no. It would not only be unfair, but it would really be offensive on my part if I did that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila has been very helpful and I really did not mean that in any way to sound offensive -- it was just the first I heard of it and I was a bit concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We were wondering about the status of admissions. We received various documents, including the last document was a letter from Mr. Fila with a letter from the Prosecutor annexed to that letter from Defence counsel. I wonder whether we could have some sort of indication of the final status of the admissions -- points which have been accepted by the Prosecutor and the admissions by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From the point of view of the Prosecution, I did not understand there to be any outstanding issues in relation to admissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am sure that is right, Mr. Niemann. Where are we going to find the finalised state. We have the letter from Mr. Fila attached to his list of admissions of 3 April. Is that the document which sets out the final state of admissions? We have attached to it your letter of 25 March. In effect, if that is right, you are not making admissions but you are not going to dispute various facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the Prosecution technically does not make admissions, but that is our position, to help Mr. Fila in the presentation of his case. In relation to the admissions agreed upon between the parties, the signed version of those have been filed and with the exception of one admission --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last admission I sent to the Prosecutor was not submitted now by the Prosecutor, so I think he should submit it -- 14 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila is right -- we are waiting for one outstanding one, for it to be signed by Mr. Dokmanovic and Mr. Fila. It has been signed and supplied to us. I can tender it now or alternatively file it in the usual way. If your Honours would like to see it, it is here. That is the original copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. If you could file it formally so we can get copies of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether there are any points any party would like to raise before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is perhaps one point. It may transpire this way in any event, bearing in mind the scheduling of the court hearings, but at the conclusion of the Defence case, in terms of evidence, if we are to embark upon any rebuttal case, we would need a short period -- nothing more than two weeks, I would think -- but a short period out of court to gather any evidence which we may need in rebuttal, should that transpire. Generally, these things work themselves out, because of the court's commitments there are delays anyway, so it often happens that way, but, when your Honours were talking about concluding in May, it was that matter that concerned me. I did not think that we would hear the end of the case and be able to conclude the case in its totality, if that were to happen that way. I should raise that at this stage, because if we are to gather rebuttal evidence, it would take a short time to do so. We are not going to remain idle on this. If issues arise during the course of the evidence that we believe needs rebutting, we will immediately embark upon that exercise through the Defence case, but it is possible that the last witnesses that are heard, we would need a little time for that. I do not see anything extensive in it. I just raise it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully appreciate Mr. Niemann's point of view and I have no objections, but, in my wish to speed up matters, according to the rules of this Tribunal, evidence is presented one after the other -- first I do, then the Prosecutor, et cetera, et cetera. Nowhere does it say we cannot reach a different kind of agreement on this matter. I am fully willing to accept that, while I am presenting evidence, if the Prosecutor thinks that something else should be presented, too, that they say so straight away. I will not oppose that. This is not against the rules, and this can be done, if the court so decides and, during that period, if the Prosecutor wants additional evidence, I suggest that we set a date immediately in June and that we conclude by then, because I take upon myself the obligation of concluding in May, and, as they say in our country, men should -- as they say in French, people should keep their word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us make an effort -- I think probably if you could conclude your case in May, then the Prosecutor may need two weeks, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: A break of two weeks in June and then we could finish in some time in June -- maybe in the second half of June. That depends on the availability of courtrooms, because we have a further problem. We now stand adjourned and we reconvene tomorrow at 8.30 sharp. (At 10.50 a.m. the matter adjourned until Tuesday, 21 April 1998 at 8.30 a.m.) 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
